title: The Capitoline Wolf (Lupa Capitolina)
originLocation: Rome, Latium, Italy
dateDisplay: 5th century BCE (traditional) or 11th–12th century CE (disputed casting)
medium: Hollow-cast bronze (twins added late 15th century CE)
creator: Unknown Etruscan or medieval Italian bronze-caster (twins attributed to Antonio del Pollaiuolo)
repository: Capitoline Museums, Rome (MC 1181)
anatomy: tense lupine stance with bared fangs
stylized curling mane along the neck
distended dugs nursing human founder-twins
description: Standing 75 cm high in hollow-cast bronze, the Capitoline She-Wolf embodies the sacred beast sent by Mars to suckle the exposed twin infants Romulus and Remus on the banks of the Tiber. Long attributed to a 5th-century BCE Veientine Etruscan workshop—though contested by thermoluminescence studies suggesting medieval recasting—its rigid posture, incised neck curls, and fierce apotropaic gaze defined Rome's foundational iconography.

title: Chimera of Arezzo
originLocation: Arezzo (ancient Arretium), Tuscany, Italy
medium: Hollow-cast lost-wax bronze
creator: Unknown Etruscan master bronze-caster
repository: National Archaeological Museum, Florence (Inv. 1)
anatomy: roaring leonine forequarters with bristling mane
wounded goat's head erupting from the spine
horned venomous serpent tail biting the goat's horn
description: Unearthed near the Porta San Lorentino in Arezzo in 1553 and inscribed 'TINSCVIL' ('dedicated to Tinia') on its right foreleg, this 80-cm Etruscan votive bronze originally confronted a lost statue of Bellerophon and Pegasus. Every sinew of the composite monster coils in agony as blood drips from the goat-head protruding mid-spine while its restored serpent-tail strikes upward.

title: Winged Horses of Tarquinia (Cavalli Alati)
originLocation: Ara della Regina Sanctuary, Tarquinia, Lazio, Italy
medium: Molded polychrome terracotta high relief
creator: Tarquinian coroplastic workshop
repository: Tarquinia National Archaeological Museum, Palazzo Vitelleschi
anatomy: harnessed equine bodies in synchronized stride
layered feathered wings sweeping from the shoulders
arched necks with cropped manes
description: Measuring 114 by 124 cm in fired terracotta, this pedimental plaque once adorned the monumental Ara della Regina temple on the Pian di Civita plateau at ancient Tarquinia. Modelled under late Classical Greek influence, the yoked pair of immortal winged horses drew a divine chariot across the heavens, symbolizing heroic apotheosis in Etruscan civic religion.

title: Trapezophoros with Two Griffins Devouring a Doe
originLocation: Ascoli Satriano (ancient Ausculum), Apulia, Italy
medium: Carved marble with original polychrome pigments
creator: Tarentine or Magna Graecian master sculptor
repository: Polo Museale di Ascoli Satriano, Foggia
commonsFile: Trapezophoros con due grifoni che sbranano una cerva.jpg
anatomy: hooked raptorial eagle beaks
polychrome feathered wings tinted rose and blue
crested dorsal spines and muscular lion hindquarters
description: Carved for an aristocratic Daunian princely tomb in southern Italy, this luxury marble table support (trapezophoros) preserves vivid ancient red, yellow, and blue mineral pigments. Two ferocious leonine griffins sink their beaks and claws into a fallen doe, translating a Near Eastern and Greek solar-guardian motif into Italic funerary pomp.

title: The Underworld Demon Tuchulcha Menacing Theseus
originLocation: Tomb of Orcus II, Monterozzi Necropolis, Tarquinia, Italy
medium: Wall fresco on lime plaster over rock-cut tufa
creator: Tarquinian tomb painter
repository: In situ, Tomb of Orcus II, Tarquinia
commonsFile: Tomb of orcus II tuchulcha and these.jpg
anatomy: hooked vulture beak and glaring eyes
pointed donkey ears rising through disheveled hair
great mottled wings and bearded venomous snakes coiled round the arms
description: Painted on the subterranean chamber wall of the Tomb of Orcus II at Tarquinia, the chthonic Etruscan daemon labeled 'Tuχulχa' lunges toward the trapped Greek hero Theseus (Θese) during a game in Hades. Combining a carrion-bird's beak, ass's ears, speckled wings, and brandished vipers, Tuchulcha exemplifies the terrifying hybridity of late Classical Etruscan underworld demonology.

title: Red-Figure Calyx-Krater Depicting the Death Demon Charun
originLocation: Vulci, Lazio, Italy
medium: Wheel-thrown red-figure terracotta with added white and yellow slip
creator: Vulcian Etruscan red-figure workshop
repository: Altes Museum, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (Inv. F 2952)
commonsFile: Etruscan Red-figure Ceramic Calyx Krater Charon, the Etruscan death demon; c. 300 BC, found in Vulci, Etruria (28732745955).jpg
anatomy: hooked nose and bestial grimacing fangs
pointed animalistic ears and wild locks
sweeping feathered wings and heavy mallet
description: Excavated at Vulci, this funerary red-figure calyx-krater portrays the Etruscan psychopomp and gatekeeper Charun striding forward in a short belted tunic. Unlike the aged Greek ferryman Charon, the Etruscan Χarun appears as a winged, fanged, hook-nosed demon wielding a heavy mallet used to unbolt—and seal—the gates of the underworld.

title: Fresco of the Winged Psychopomp Vanth
originLocation: Tomb of the Anina, Monterozzi Necropolis, Tarquinia, Italy
medium: Polychrome wall fresco on tufa plaster
creator: Tarquinian Hellenistic tomb painter
repository: In situ, Tomb of the Anina, Tarquinia
anatomy: vast polychrome wings framing a female torso
crossed leather baldrics leaving the chest bare
blazing funerary torch illuminating the underworld path
description: Flanking the entrance inside the aristocratic Tomb of the Anina at Tarquinia opposite her monstrous counterpart Charun, the female underworld spirit Vanth stands sentinel holding a flaming torch. Adorned with high-laced hunting boots, crossed shoulder straps, and expansive feathered wings, Vanth served as a benevolent guide escorting newly departed souls safely into the realm of Aita.

title: Pillar Fresco of the Serpent-Legged Giant Typhon
originLocation: Tomb of the Typhon, Monterozzi Necropolis, Tarquinia, Italy
medium: Fresco on plastered rock-cut central pillar
creator: Late Hellenistic Tarquinian painter
repository: In situ, Tomb of the Typhon, Tarquinia
anatomy: muscular athletic human torso straining upward
great backswept wings emerging from the scapulae
twin writhing serpent-legs terminating in bearded snake heads
description: Painted onto the central load-bearing pier of the Tomb of the Pumpu family at Tarquinia, this dynamic Hellenistic fresco depicts a winged anguiped giant acting as an architectural telamon supporting the ceiling. Dramatic chiaroscuro modeling highlights his twisting torso and coiling, crested serpent legs, fusing Pergamene gigantomachy conventions with Etruscan funerary cosmology.

title: Athena and Nike Slaying the Winged Giant Alkyoneus
originLocation: Great Altar of Pergamon, Mysia, Asia Minor (modern Bergama, Turkey)
medium: High-relief Proconnesian marble frieze
creator: Royal Attalid sculptural workshops of Pergamon
repository: Pergamon Museum, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
commonsFile: Athena & Nike, East Frieze, Gigantomachy Frieze, Pergamon Altar, Pergamon Museum, Berlin (5912953449).jpg
anatomy: heroically muscled humanoid body contorted in pain
broad feathered wings spread behind the shoulders
earth-born chthonic kinship with coiled sacred serpents
description: Carved in tumultuous high relief on the east Gigantomachy frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon—celebrated in Roman antiquity as a marvel of the province of Asia—Athena yanks the winged Giant Alkyoneus by the hair to sever his immortalizing contact with his mother Gaia rising below. Athena's sacred serpent sinks its fangs into the Giant's chest as winged Nike crowns the victorious goddess.

title: Polyphemus and Galatea in a Sacro-Idyllic Landscape
originLocation: Mythological Room, Villa of Agrippa Postumus, Boscotrecase, Campania, Italy
medium: Buon fresco on lime plaster
creator: Imperial Augustan Campanian workshop
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (20.192.17)
commonsFile: Wall painting- Polyphemus and Galatea in a landscape, from the imperial villa at Boscotrecase MET DP140711.jpg
anatomy: colossal sun-bronzed giant's physique
central third eye on the brow
rustic panpipes and gnarled shepherd's staff
description: Recovered from the imperial villa of Augustus's grandson Agrippa Postumus on the slopes of Mount Vesuvius, this refined Third Style fresco merges two episodes of the Cyclops myth within one atmospheric seascape. In the foreground, a lovesick Polyphemus sits on a crag clutching his syrinx to serenade the sea-nymph Galatea riding a dolphin, while in the misty background he hurls boulders at Odysseus's fleeing ship.

title: Perseus Rescuing Andromeda from the Sea-Monster Cetus
originLocation: Mythological Room, Villa of Agrippa Postumus, Boscotrecase, Campania, Italy
medium: Buon fresco on lime plaster
creator: Imperial Augustan Campanian workshop
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (20.192.16)
commonsFile: Wall painting- Perseus and Andromeda in landscape, from the imperial villa at Boscotrecase MET DT5194.jpg
anatomy: gaping wolf-like crocodilian jaws lined with teeth
spiny aquatic crest and pectoral fins
coiling serpentine sea-dragon body emerging from the waves
description: Paired opposite the Polyphemus panel in the imperial villa at Boscotrecase, this Augustan wall painting stages Andromeda chained to a towering sea-cliff at center while Perseus flies in on winged sandals from the right. At lower left, the abyssal sea-monster Cetus—dispatched by Poseidon—rears its fanged, crested dragon-snout from the dark green surf toward its intended victim.

title: Gemma Augustea Featuring the Imperial Sea-Goat Capricorn
originLocation: Rome, Italy
medium: Two-layered Arabian onyx cameo in later openwork gold mount
creator: Attributed to Dioskourides or his imperial workshop
repository: Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna (Antikensammlung IXa 79)
anatomy: horned caprine head and forelegs
looped scaly fish tail
radiant eight-pointed star framed within a celestial disc
description: Carved in crisp milky-white relief over a dark brown onyx ground, the 19-by-23-cm Gemma Augustea exalts Emperor Augustus enthroned beside the goddess Roma. Floating above Augustus's brow in a solar medallion is the hybrid sea-goat Capricorn—his personal natal zodiacal sign—proclaiming cosmic destiny over land and sea alike.

title: The Scylla Group from the Imperial Grotto of Sperlonga
originLocation: Grotto of Tiberius, Sperlonga, Lazio, Italy
medium: Carved marble monumental sculpture group
creator: Signed by the Rhodian sculptors Athanadoros, Hagesandros, and Polydoros
repository: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Sperlonga
anatomy: colossal female upper torso gripping the ship's steering-oar
pack of snarling canine heads sprouting from the groin
coiling pisciform tails dragging sailors into the whirlpool
description: Originally erected on an artificial island at the center of Emperor Tiberius's flooded banquet cave at Sperlonga and signed by the same Rhodian trio credited by Pliny with the Laocoön, this monumental marble group captures Scylla's assault on Odysseus's ship. While the monster's giant hand seizes the helmsman by the scalp, ferocious dog-foreparts lunging from her waist devour his companions.

title: Grand Camée de France with the Winged Horse Pegasus
originLocation: Rome, Italy
medium: Five-layered sardonyx cameo
creator: Imperial Julio-Claudian court gem-cutter
repository: Cabinet des Médailles, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (Camée 264)
commonsFile: Great Cameo of France CdM Paris Bab264 n1.jpg
anatomy: rearing stallion carved in translucent white sardonyx
upswept avian wings bearing an imperial rider
celestial gallop guided by a flying Amor
description: Measuring 31 by 26.5 cm, the five-layered Grand Camée de France is the largest surviving imperial cameo from Classical antiquity, structured into three cosmic tiers: captive barbarians below, Tiberius and Livia enthroned at center, and the deified Augustus in heaven above. Rising into the upper register on the winged stallion Pegasus is the deceased prince Germanicus, carried skyward toward imperial apotheosis.

title: Theseus Honored After Slaying the Minotaur
originLocation: Exedra of the House of M. Gavius Rufus (VII 2, 16), Pompeii, Italy
medium: Wall fresco detached from plaster
creator: Pompeian Fourth Style painter
repository: National Archaeological Museum, Naples (MANN Inv. 9043)
anatomy: horned bovine bull's head and thick neck
heavy muscular human body sprawled at the Labyrinth threshold
clenched human hands in rigor
description: Excavated in the House of Marcus Gavius Rufus at Pompeii and modeled after a celebrated Greek painting, this Fourth Style fresco shows Athenian youths kissing the hand and knees of a victorious Theseus. Sprawled across the lower left doorway of the Cretan Labyrinth lies the corpse of the bull-headed Minotaur, foreshortened to contrast bestial monstrosity with heroic civic deliverance.

title: Pan Teaching the Shepherd Daphnis to Play the Syrinx
originLocation: Pompeii, Campania, Italy
dateDisplay: 1st century CE (after a c. 100 BCE Hellenistic original)
medium: Carved white marble
creator: Roman sculptor after Heliodoros of Rhodes
repository: National Archaeological Museum, Naples (Farnese/Pompeian collection)
anatomy: shaggy caprine thighs and cloven goat hooves
sprouting goat horns and pointed satyr-ears
furrowed bestial brow and bearded muzzle
description: Replicating a celebrated late Hellenistic symplegma attributed to Heliodoros, this marble sculpture group contrasts the supple, idealized youth of the mortal shepherd Daphnis with the gnarly, goat-legged woodland god Pan seated beside him. Pan twists his horned head and shaggy hindquarters toward the boy to guide his fingers across the reed panpipes.

title: Battle of Centaurs and Wild Cats of Prey
originLocation: Triclinium of Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli, Lazio, Italy
medium: Opus vermiculatum polychrome stone and glass tesserae
creator: Hadrianic mosaicists after a Hellenistic original
repository: Altes Museum, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (Mos. 1)
commonsFile: Centaur mosaic - Google Art Project retouched.jpeg
anatomy: youthful human torso hoisting a jagged boulder
dappled chestnut equine barrel and rearing forelegs
windswept leopard-skin cloak knotted at the throat
description: Executed in microscopic opus vermiculatum tesserae for a banquet hall at Emperor Hadrian's Villa in Tivoli, this 58-by-91-cm emblemata panel achieves painterly gradations of light and shadow across a rocky mountain pass. A male centaur rears above his mortally mauled female companion—who lies bleeding beneath a tiger—as he prepares to crush an attacking lion and leopard with a boulder.

title: The Old Furietti Centaur
originLocation: Hadrian's Villa, Tivoli, Lazio, Italy
medium: Polished dark grey-black bigio morato marble
creator: Signed by Aristeas and Papias of Aphrodisias
repository: Capitoline Museums, Palazzo Nuovo, Rome (MC 658)
anatomy: bearded, anguished human face crowned with ivy
arms wrenched taut behind a muscular human back
glossy dark-marble equine body and prancing hooves
description: Discovered at Hadrian's Villa in 1736 by Monsignor Giuseppe Alessandro Furietti alongside its jubilant 'Young Centaur' counterpart, this virtuoso statue is signed on the plinth by the Carian masters Aristeas and Papias of Aphrodisias. Carved from lustrous dark bigio morato marble to imitate patinated Hellenistic bronze, the aged centaur winces in torment with his wrists bound behind his back by an unseen Eros.

title: Amphitrite Riding a Hippocampus Among Tritons
originLocation: Room 3, Baths of Neptune, Ostia Antica, Lazio, Italy
medium: Black-and-white limestone and marble floor mosaic
creator: Ostian mosaic workshop under Antoninus Pius
repository: In situ, Terme di Nettuno, Parco Archeologico di Ostia Antica
commonsFile: Amphitrite Terme di Nettuno Ostia Antica 2006-09-08.jpg
anatomy: bridled equine forequarters with webbed fin-hooves
elongated looping serpentine fish-tail
attendant fish-tailed Tritons blowing conch shells
description: Spanning an entire bathing hall in Rome's port city of Ostia Antica, this monumental Antonine black-and-white pavement celebrates the marine thiasos of Queen Amphitrite. Preceded by winged Hymenaios, the sea-goddess reclines with billowing veil astride a spirited Hippocampus whose horse-chest dissolves into undulating sea-serpent coils surrounded by horn-blowing Tritons.

title: Cult Statue of the Prophetic Serpent-God Glycon
originLocation: Tomis (modern Constanța), Romania
medium: Single-block carved white marble
creator: Provincial Pontic-Roman sculptor
repository: Museum of National History and Archeology, Constanța
anatomy: anthropomorphic-ovine snout with long flowing human locks
tightly wound concentric coils of scaly serpent body
tufted leonine tail raised behind the head
description: Unearthed in 1962 in a ritual cache beneath the former railway station of Constanța (ancient Tomis) and sculpted from a single block of marble whose coiled length measures 4.76 meters, this unique cult statue depicts Glycon—the 'New Asclepius' introduced around 150 CE by the prophet Alexander of Abonoteichus. Combining a long-haired anthropomorphic-ovine head, intricately crosshatched snake coils, and a lion's tail-tuft, it confirms Lucian of Samosata's eyewitness account of the oracle cult.

title: Mithraic Lion-Headed Time-God (Leontocephaline Aion)
originLocation: Mithraeum at Ostia Antica, Lazio, Italy
medium: Carved white marble
creator: Roman Mithraic workshop (dedicated by C. Valerius Heracles)
repository: Museo Chiaramonti / Gregorian Profane Museum, Vatican Museums
anatomy: roaring maned lion's head atop a rigid human body
four seasonal wings sprouting from back and hips
giant cosmic serpent spiraling multiple turns up the legs and torso
description: Dedicated in 190 CE at an Ostian Mithraeum by the priest Caius Valerius Heracles, this esoteric marble cult statue embodies infinite cosmic time (Aion) within the Roman Mysteries of Mithras. A roaring lion-headed man stands at attention clutching the keys of the celestial gates while a colossal serpent—charting the sun's ecliptic path through the zodiac—winds tightly up his legs and rests its head upon his mane.

title: Architectural Medallion with Head of the Gorgon Medusa
originLocation: Severan Forum, Leptis Magna, Tripolitania (modern Libya)
medium: Deeply drilled Proconnesian marble arcade spandrel
creator: Aphrodisian sculptors in imperial service under Septimius Severus
repository: In situ, Severan Forum, Leptis Magna, Libya
anatomy: petrifying wide-eyed gaze beneath furrowed brows
billowing mane of deeply undercut locks and writhing snakes
pair of serpent tails knotted beneath the chin and head-wings above
description: Commissioned by the African-born Emperor Septimius Severus to monumentalize his native city of Leptis Magna, scores of colossal marble Gorgoneia and Nereid medallions punctuated the colonnaded arcades of the Severan Forum. Deep running-drill channels cast stark African sunlight and shadow across Medusa's tempestuous locks, brow-wings, and chin-knotted vipers, turning the imperial plaza into an apotropaic shield.

title: Mosaic of Odysseus Resisting the Bird-Bodied Sirens
originLocation: House of Dionysus and Ulysses, Dougga (ancient Thugga), Tunisia
medium: Polychrome limestone and marble tesserae
creator: Romano-African mosaic workshop of Thugga
repository: Bardo National Museum, Tunis
anatomy: female busts and coiffed heads playing double pipes and lyre
feathered bird-wings folded against the flanks
long scaled raptor legs and taloned feet perched on sea-rocks
description: Lifted from an aristocratic peristyle house at Thugga in Roman Africa Proconsularis, this 3.8-meter polychrome pavement depicts Ulysses lashed upright to the mainmast of his gilded, oar-banked galley. Perched on wave-lapped crags to the right stand three hybrid Sirens—women from the waist up with feathered wings and tall raptorial bird-legs—playing aulos and lyre in vain.

title: Pavement Mosaic of the Haloed Phoenix on a Field of Roses
originLocation: House of the Phoenix, Daphne (suburb of Antioch-on-the-Orontes, modern Antakya, Turkey)
medium: Marble and limestone polychrome floor mosaic
creator: Antiochene mosaic workshop
repository: Musée du Louvre, Paris (Ma 3442 / MND 1948)
anatomy: radiant solar nimbus with seven projecting rays
curved crest-plume and long crane-like legs
iridescent grey-green plumage standing atop a stepped crag
description: Excavated in 1934 at Daphne outside Antioch-on-the-Orontes, this monumental 6-by-4.25-meter pavement centers on the immortal solar bird Phoenix standing atop a rocky pinnacle amid an infinite carpet of rosebuds and stepped rams' horns. Crowned by a rayed nimbus borrowed from Sol Invictus and adopted into Roman imperial coinage as 'FELIX TEMPORUM REPARATIO', the Antiochene Phoenix bridges pagan solar eternity and Early Christian resurrection symbolism.

title: Peristyle Floor Mosaic of the Winged Lion-Griffin
originLocation: Great Palace of Constantinople, Istanbul, Turkey
dateDisplay: 6th century CE (Reign of Justinian I or Justin II)
medium: Limestone, terracotta, and colored glass tesserae on mortar
creator: Imperial Constantinopolitan palace mosaicists
repository: Great Palace Mosaic Museum, Istanbul
anatomy: tawny leonine body with striped feline musculature
aquiline raptor head and pointed ears
polychrome green-and-crimson wings set against a white scale-ground
description: Laid with roughly 40,000 five-millimeter tesserae per square meter across the open peristyle courtyard of the Byzantine emperors' Great Palace in Constantinople, this Early Byzantine floor mosaic preserves Classical naturalism against an abstract fan-patterned white ground. The striding winged lion-griffin radiates sovereign vigilance alongside nearby vignettes of tiger-griffins, Bellerophon's Chimera, and exotic hunts.

title: Shroud of Saint Germain of Auxerre (Imperial Byzantine Eagle Silk)
originLocation: Imperial gynecaeum workshops, Constantinople (preserved at Auxerre, France)
medium: Samite silk woven with murex-purple, dark blue, and yellow silk threads
creator: Imperial silk workshops of Constantinople
repository: Abbey of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre, France
commonsFile: Abbaye Saint-Germain d'Auxerre-Suaire de saint Germain (1).jpg
anatomy: monumental heraldic wings patterned with rosettes and hearts
jeweled ring and pendant clutched in the hooked beak
fanned tail feathers and taloned feet poised on stepped pedestals
description: Woven in coveted imperial purple samite in the court workshops of Constantinople around 1000 CE and later brought west to wrap the relics of Saint Germain at Auxerre, this 160-by-120-cm silk ranks among the finest surviving Macedonian-era textiles. Colossal heraldic eagles with rosette-studded plumage hold precious gemmed rings in their beaks, embodying the celestial sovereignty of the Byzantine basileus.

title: Celestial Flight of Alexander the Great Drawn by Two Griffins
originLocation: Constantinople (installed as spolia on the north facade of San Marco, Venice)
medium: Carved marble architectural relief plaque
creator: Middle Byzantine Constantinopolitan sculptor
repository: Exterior north facade, Basilica di San Marco, Venice
anatomy: symmetrical pair of rampant winged griffins
straining eagle heads snapping upward toward baited spears
muscular lion bodies harnessed to a celestial chariot-basket
description: Brought from Constantinople to Venice—likely after the Fourth Crusade of 1204—and set into the north exterior wall of San Marco, this Middle Byzantine marble relief illustrates the legendary 'Ascent of Alexander' from the Greek Alexander Romance. Wearing the jeweled loros and crown of a Byzantine emperor, Alexander stands in a chariot-basket holding out two skewered animal livers on spears to lure a pair of hungry, harnessed griffins ever higher into the sky.

title: Icon of the Miracle of Saint George and the Dragon ('Black George')
originLocation: Novgorod Republic (in the Late Byzantine iconographic tradition)
dateDisplay: First half of the 15th century CE (c. 1400–1450)
medium: Egg tempera and gesso on wooden panel
creator: Byzantine-tradition iconographer of Novgorod
repository: British Museum, London (1986,0603.1)
commonsFile: Black St George Icon - Joy of Museums.jpg
anatomy: crested serpentine dragon head pierced through the jaws
bat-like red-and-ochre wings emerging above two clawed forelegs
knotted tail coiling out of a subterranean abyssal lair
description: Painted in luminous vermilion, cinnabar, and black egg tempera on a carved limewood panel, the celebrated 'Black George' icon adapts Eastern Christian Byzantine dragon-slayer iconography to its starkest silhouette. Astride a jet-black steed blessed by the hand of God from an arc of heaven, the haloed warrior-saint drives his cross-topped lance straight into the gaping maw of a winged, two-legged serpentine dragon emerging from a dark cavern.
